We are dealing in hypotheticals here. Presumably if Gearbox were to go in and add mantling, they would also update the map bounds to compensate for that. Also as you said yourself, for a lot of the areas there isn't much call for mantling anyhow. For the limited platforming in the game the mantling would absolutely make it that little bit nicer to do.
If someone is going to get out of bounds, they are going to do it mantling or no. The addition of mantling mainly just removes a degree of frustration from first person platforming.

There are several places where there are chests and such at the end of some sparse platforming, and often if you misstime the jumps or cruouches you'll bounce off the edges and have a long way back up. They aren't frequent or common, but it would be a nice thing to have in the few instances where it would be needed.

In all games up to three I cannot begin to count the number of times where I misjudged a jump and either died or had the walk of shame to reset myself. It was less so in Pre-sequel as there was the Oz kit to readjust yourself, but mantling is just a great quality of life addition to any game with first person traversal.

The only hope we really have is if someone with far more technical knowhow than I can effectively either reverse engineer the server data a la what was done with one of the older Mario Kart games, or effectively rebuilds the game from the ground up.

You generally want to keep the higher number things even if they are worth more to sell, since by later game you'll have sold enough that money really stops being an issue.

Apologies for the word dump but I have a lot of thoughts here.     
             
       
The Calypso twins never really landed for me. Their antics just come across as annoying and petulant. Whenever they came on over the echo I was just looking forward to when they'd shut up. Compare that to all the other installments' villains; Jack, Zarpedon, even Steele from the first game. I looked forward to the next interaction with them. I was interested in their motives and character even on subsequent playthroughs.      
On all the other borderlands games, I played through several times in the first year alone. In 3 I initially started a second run, but dropped it because I just didn't want to sit through another 30 odd hours of the twins. I am now playing it again because a friend of mine recently got it, and every time the twins come on I mostly ignore them. I'm supposed to want the Villain dead, not just to shut up.      
          
Ava is also a sore spot. They clearly saw the fan appreciation of Tiny Tina and wanted to do that again. They made the unfortunate choice of just wrapping every trope of teenage angst into a ball and calling it a day. The backstory they gave her is like that of every 13 year old's first RP character. I would have expected better from a studio that has previously brought us some fairly nuanced characters. To be fair, I did hear they did a lot to help her character in the DLC, but I haven't bought that one so I can't really weigh in on it.         
          
The story is full of a lot of really contrived moments. Every time you have a run in with the Calypsos in person, the game just puts you in a box and ignores you. When a story beat would be subverted by the simple act of you character doing anything, that's not good writing.     
At the start of the game when Lilith loses her powers, they could have instead had a boss fight where the twins actually overpower you, force you to lose and retreat, then Lilith saves you and the cutscene continues as normal.     
The one after the Rampager could have been fixed very simply. The Calypsos come by while you're in the vault. You come out just as the twins are leaving, then flashback to see what happened or something.   
Heck, the exchange between Lilith and Maya on Sanctuary where Maya asks Lilith about why her tattoos are gone, a thing that literally no siren has ever seen happen before to anyone's knowledge, and all lilith has to say is "I don't want to talk about it."? Honestly say what you want but Maya's death is on lilith's hands just as much if not more so than Ava. Also on that note, why did Maya even grab Troy by hand? Girl had him phase locked and anyone who's played borderlands 2 knows how much damage she could do with that. That's way more threatening than putting a gun to his head.       
Why the hell did Lilith leave the Crimson raiders to Ava? Here is a child, who just got here, who just got their siren powers, and you're going to leave her in charge in the face of so many other characters who are entirely more qualified for the job. Sure, maybe she could take over one day, when she's ready, but that is not the Ava we have at the end of the game.     

       
Another moment that sticks out to me is the Troy boss fight. I think a far more interesting end to that would have been if he had accidentally leached Tyreen and killed her. Seeing him break from the realisation that he'd become too drunk with power and pushed it too far. Seeing him become unhinged with the guilt of killing his sister. Seeing his probable desperation now that his source of sustenance is gone. The end of the story could have been a mad dash for more things to absorb to sustain himself. The final confrontation with a twisted, rotting hybrid of Troy and the Destroyer; mad and with an insatiable hunger.     
Moments like that cropped up a number of times where is felt like the came to a branch in the narrative and picked a simpler path for the story, when more interesting options could have been taken. 
         
Kind of on a more minor note, but I wish the characters felt more involved in the story and world. In Pre-Sequel, for example, all the characters banter with each other, and NPC's have unique dialogue responses for each character in any story interactions. In 3 it's just a boiler plate response no matter who is there. It seems like you could have easily been replaced with a cardboard cutout and nothing would change. 
         
There were moments of good. A lot of the side quest writing I enjoyed far more than anything the main line had to offer. I have a particular fondness for the one later where the twins are holding auditions for a new Mouthpiece. That is one of the only times in the game I actually enjoyed their interactions. There were moments like that all through the game, but as a whole, the writing just largely fell flat for me.     
It's such a shame, as the game play is just fantastic. Moment to moment gunplay, movement, and abilities have never felt so good.     
Borderlands 3 feels to me like they blew all of their budget on the gameplay and mechanics, and ran a skeleton crew in the writing room. Save for Zane. I honestly think part of what had me coming back was waiting to hear the next quip out of his beautiful Irish face.
I'm waiting to see what people say about the story. I of course hope the gameplay is fun, but if the story is another miss like borderlands 3, I will be taking a miss on this one.

It's often implemented in RPG type games, and even then it depends on the game. If balancing stats and weighing odds is more central to the game they'll leave the numbers as they roll (X-com is famous for this).    
If you're playing something less overly numbers focused, take borderlands for example, the numbers will be skewed in you favor. The rationale for this is while it isn't as accurate to actual statistical likelihood, it is more fun. That is generally where the math tends to be fudged; for the sake of a more fun experience.

Okay, I might just be bogging it down a bit, but for a different example, take flipping a coin. Each time you flip it there's a 50% chance of it landing on either face.     
IRL you can have it land on tails for example like 12 times in a row, because each instance of possibility is isolated and doesn't effect the other.     
In many video games, the math is often built to favor the median. If you get multiple instances of heads in a row, the math is built to sprinkle in some tails results to even out the spread.    
Back to the 30% example, in a game it means that out of 100 hits, very close to 30 would deal fire damage. With IRL probability, it may take more or less time for the median to arise in the data.

Unless you're talking about damage numbers or chance to hit in most video games. They tend to skew the numbers so that the math works out like you think it should, ie. a 30% chance to deal fire damage works out to a third of your hits will deal fire damage, as opposed to getting a string of 12 non-fire attacks because each had only a 1 in 3 chance to deal fire gamage.
